extracted.intended_audience: beginner and amateur naturalists / conchologists (school students, collectors)
extracted.subtask_short: collecting and preserving land & freshwater shells
extracted.subtask_description: Practical field and preparatory guidance for finding, collecting, identifying, and preserving British land and freshwater molluscs (snails, slugs, mussels) aimed at beginners and amateur naturalists. Covers habitat selection, field methods, specimen selection, transport, cleaning, preservation, and basic identification tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of magnifying glass and microscope for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: A magnifying glass, for the dissection of inward parts, is necessary in many cases to separate two kinds which look alike. If you possess, or borrow, a microscope, many new wonders and fresh lines of inquiry will open out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small shells may require magnifying glass or microscope to distinguish markings, sculpture, and species. Microscopy enables study of teeth (radula), minute anatomical points, and life-history from egg onwards; specialists may examine radula teeth counts and structure (e.g. thousands of teeth on a ribbon) to determine species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate habitats (lime/chalk preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Snails require lime to make shells, and only on chalk or limestone will you find an abundance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer chalk/limestone areas (e.g. Caterham, Box Hill) for large Helices like Helix pomatia. Seek hedges, moss-covered tree bases, walls, beech boles, damp places, and ditches depending on species and season.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal timing and search locations
rubrics_metrics.description: In the hibernating season (November to April) we turn rather to ditches than to hedges; rainy days and warm evenings are favourable; night searches with a lantern may be profitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for epiphragms and discarded winter 'front doors' in early summer; search trunks (smooth beeches), under stones/wood/boots/newspaper, in hedges, and under dead leaves. Use different locations by season (hedges & trees in summer, ditches/ponds in winter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field searching methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn over stones, bricks, branches, old boots, or papers; sweep herbage with a net or beat hedges over an inverted umbrella; set traps such as flat pieces of wood or cardboard; night search with lantern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many smaller shells are found by turning over cover objects. Be thorough: 'leave no stone unturned.' Some species favour newspapers as shelter/food. Traps (old wood, cardboard) can attract snails; use entomological beating methods for shrubs as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aquatic collecting methods (dredging & sifting)
rubrics_metrics.description: During hibernating season use a perforated scoop at the end of a long stick to dredge among water-weeds, or sift sand or mud in ditches, ponds, and backwaters of rivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dredge and sift to reach bivalves and aquatic gasteropods. Observe cases of caddis-worms to infer small shell inhabitants. Freshwater specimens can often be brought home alive in a tin box with a little moss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport: calico bags, tin boxes, and glass tubes
rubrics_metrics.description: For land shells a calico bag with a little foliage is best. Freshwater shells can be brought home alive in a tin box with a little moss. Small glass tubes with corks should be brought to keep the tinier kinds separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pack specimens to avoid damage and mixing. Use separate small tubes for tiny shells to protect them and preserve identity of locality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kill method for preserving shells
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash of quite boiling water kills instantaneously any molluscs whose shells we want to preserve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After killing, extract the body and clean the shell promptly. Boiling water is advised for shells intended to be kept as specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning shells (remove body and slime)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to get out all the body of the animal, and then it is well to wash out any slime or particles by directing a fine but strong jet of cold water into the shell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: hold the shell in left hand and nearly cover the tap with the thumb to direct a fine, strong jet. Ensure all slime is removed before drying or mounting; only adult shells should usually be taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select adult, undamaged specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Only adult shells should usually be taken, and those which are weather-worn or bleached should be neglected. In most the lip, or opening, of the shell will be hard if adult, and membranous if young.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience is required to discriminate adult from juvenile in cases where young of one species resemble adults of another. Prefer specimens with intact apertures and good colour/pattern for study and display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry a field notebook and record observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Get into the way of carrying a note-book with you to record not only what shells, or varieties of a species, are found in any particular spot, but also anything you observe as to the habits or peculiarities of the objects of your search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record protective colouring, mimicry, seasonal influences on shell thickness, size variation with diet, preferred foodplants, earliest/latest active dates, and precise locality data to add scientific value to collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of slugs (best practice: drawing)
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve slugs is difficult, and the best plan is to have a coloured drawing made of them when extended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative preservation: drown, clean slime with a soft brush, and preserve in glass tubes with diluted formalin or alcohol; or drown, skin and dry the skins on a card and varnish. Note many slugs vary in colour and markings, so drawings record natural appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anatomy and internal characters for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: A microscope and dissection may determine by minute anatomical points whether two molluscs were of the same species or not--a matter in which the shape or appearance of the shell is not always a safe guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study love-darts, dart shape differences (e.g. H. nemoralis vs H. hortensis), radula teeth counts/structure, muscular scars, and mantle/anatomical features when shells are similar externally. Dissection may be needed to separate closely allied species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn shell and body terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Use plate/diagram to understand certain names of parts of the shell or the body of the bivalve, univalve, or slug which otherwise might not be clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know terms such as epiphragm, operculum, umbilicus, mouth/aperture, mantle, muscular scars, whorls, pillar lip. Familiarity with terms aids accurate description and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner species focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginners' attention should first be directed to the two allied species Helix (Cepea) nemoralis and H. hortensis, inasmuch as they are so common, so beautiful, and so varying both in colour and the number of the chocolate bands they usually bear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These species are useful for learning variation in colour and banding; their study teaches observation of intraspecific variation and identification practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storage and arrangement of collections
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to make a collection, whether of dried plants, of insects, of shells, or of anything else, you must cultivate ways of order and method and neatness in the arrangement of your collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make wall-cases (example given for a school) containing specimens arranged systematically; orderliness aids later study and comparison and builds good scientific habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate killing/preservation for different groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Freshwater shells can be brought home alive in a tin box with a little moss, whereas for the land shells a calico bag with a little foliage therein is best. For slugs, drowning and preserving in diluted formalin or alcohol is advised; some slugs may be skinned and dried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor transport and preservation to the physiology and fragility of the animal: bivalves tolerate being kept alive; delicate Vitrina-like shells need careful handling; slugs require specific chemical preservation or drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for diagnostic incidental evidence (epiphragms, love-darts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Look about on the grass for some half-chalky, half-stony shields, which are the winter front doors of H. pomatia, now discarded; while sharper eyes might even descry the flinty little darts with which they have been love-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such incidental findings (epiphragms, love-darts) can aid locating species and can be diagnostic (dart morphology can distinguish closely allied species). Examine ground cover carefully for these signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-collecting juveniles; aim for complete but responsible collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Some are as small as a pin's head although full grown... Here, however, is no impossible ideal of perfection. There are but eighty-two land and forty-five freshwater shells in Britain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because species counts are limited, collectors can hope to form complete sets; nonetheless collectors should generally take adults and avoid unnecessary depletion of local populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult reference works and experienced collectors
rubrics_metrics.description: If you must fall back upon a book, get The Collector's Manual by L. E. Adams... If any collector lives near you, I am sure he or she would be delighted to have your company during an expedition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authoritative manuals and learn in the field with experienced collectors to accelerate learning; borrow plates and diagrams for beginners to understand morphology.
